title: Lymphatic System Anatomy: Nodes, Thoracic Duct & Organs
description: Learn lymphatic system anatomy, tracing lymph capillaries, regional lymph node chains, the cisterna chyli, thoracic duct drainage, thymus, and spleen pulp.
h1: Lymphatic System Anatomy: Vessels, Lymph Nodes, Ducts and Immunity
blurb: One-way lymphatic capillaries, filtering cervical, axillary, and inguinal node chains, the thoracic duct, thymus, and spleen working together for fluid and immunity.
lead: Every day, several liters of fluid filter out of blood capillaries into body tissues; the lymphatic system collects that fluid, screens it through immune nodes, and returns it to veins. In this illustrated guide to lymphatic system anatomy, we examine 20 documented structures—including cervical nodes, axillary nodes, inguinal nodes, thoracic duct—linking regional topography, tissue architecture, physiological mechanisms, and clinical reasoning.
overview: Every day, several liters of fluid filter out of blood capillaries into body tissues; the lymphatic system collects that fluid, screens it through immune nodes, and returns it to veins. Node groups, trunks and the organs of immunity — with the clinical rule that nodes enlarge downstream of infection and cancer. Within the human body, the lymphatic system (Systema lymphoideum) is situated in whole body, receives arterial perfusion via returns via subclavian veins, and is innervated by autonomic on vessels.

Structurally, the cervical nodes (Ll. cervicales) comprises chains along jugular and spine. Physiologically, the cervical nodes drain head and neck. The axillary nodes (Ll. axillares) are five groups in the armpit. Physiologically, the axillary nodes drain arm, breast and chest wall. Structurally, the inguinal nodes (Ll. inguinales) comprises horizontal + vertical groups in the groin. Physiologically, the inguinal nodes drain leg, perineum and lower abdominal wall. Structurally, the thoracic duct (Ductus thoracicus) comprises largest lymph channel, cisterna chyli to left venous angle. Physiologically, the thoracic duct returns 3/4 of body lymph. Structurally, the thymus comprises bilobed school for T cells, behind sternum. Physiologically, the thymus governs t-cell maturation in childhood. Structurally, the spleen (Splen / Lien) comprises largest lymphoid organ, left upper quadrant. Physiologically, the spleen filters blood; recycles iron; antibodies.

Clinically, regarding the cervical nodes, rubbery vs hard-fixed distinguishes infection from malignancy. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the axillary nodes, sentinel node first receives breast cancer cells. In clinical pathology involving the inguinal nodes, enlarge in leg infections and STIs. Medical evaluation of the thoracic duct also notes that chylothorax if torn in chest surgery.

questions.question: What does the lymphatic system do?
questions.answer: It returns excess interstitial fluid to the bloodstream, transports absorbed fats from the intestine and supports immune surveillance through nodes and lymphoid organs.

questions.question: Where does lymph drain back into the blood?
questions.answer: The major lymphatic ducts empty near the junctions of the internal jugular and subclavian veins; the thoracic duct drains most of the body.

questions.question: Where are the cervical lymph nodes located?
questions.answer: Cervical lymph nodes are arranged in chains along the internal jugular vessels and through the posterior neck.

questions.question: Where are the inguinal lymph nodes located?
questions.answer: Inguinal lymph nodes form superficial horizontal and vertical groups in the groin.

questions.question: What is the function of the thymus?
questions.answer: The thymus supports T-lymphocyte maturation, especially during childhood; it lies behind the sternum.
